new_entities.name: Chronic high-dose acetaminophen
new_entities.description: Repeated acetaminophen exposure at or near the upper recommended daily dose over multiple consecutive days.

new_entities.name: Liver enzyme elevation
new_entities.description: Elevation of aminotransferases such as ALT or AST during drug exposure.

edges.effect_quant: The anchor randomized trial in healthy adults found ALT above three times the upper limit of normal in 31% to 44% of participants receiving 4 g/day, whereas a broader systematic review of 30,865 prospectively observed subjects found aminotransferase elevations in only 0.4% overall and no fulminant hepatic failure.
edges.population: adults exposed to repeated acetaminophen dosing at or near 4 g/day, including healthy volunteers and newly abstinent alcohol-dependent patients
edges.mechanism: When high daily acetaminophen dosing is repeated over consecutive days, hepatotoxic metabolite production can outpace glutathione buffering enough to raise aminotransferases before overt liver failure appears.
edges.summary: The literature supports a real laboratory liver-signal edge at sustained high therapeutic dosing, but it is not the same as saying routine short-course use reliably causes clinical liver failure. The best evidence shows that aminotransferase elevations can appear surprisingly often in tightly monitored healthy volunteers at 4 g/day, while other short-duration or special-population studies show much milder findings.
edges.caveats: Duration, fasting status, alcohol timing, and exact dose matter. This edge is about laboratory enzyme elevations during repeated high-dose exposure, not proof that every therapeutic course causes clinically meaningful liver injury.

evidence.notes: Aminotransferase elevations in healthy adults receiving 4 grams of acetaminophen daily: a randomized controlled trial.
